title: Ruth, Hannah and Samuel
bigQuestion: How do the stories of Ruth, Hannah and Samuel show loyalty and kindness, and how did Israel come to ask for a king?

story.title: A Promise on a Dusty Road
story.kicker: Three women stand at a crossroads. One is going home. The other two must choose.
paragraphs: The road is dry and dusty. It runs from the land of Moab toward Bethlehem, a town in the hills of Judah. An old woman named Naomi stands on the road. Two young women stand with her. They are her sons' wives. Her sons have died. Her husband has died. She has nothing left in Moab.

Naomi turns to the two young women. Their names are Orpah and Ruth. Go back, she tells them. Go home to your mothers. You are young. You can marry again. I am old and I have nothing to give you. She kisses them. All three of them cry.

Orpah kisses Naomi and turns back toward Moab. She has made her choice, and the book of Ruth does not blame her. But Ruth does not move. She holds on to Naomi. Naomi tells her again to go. Ruth answers with words that people still say today.

Do not ask me to leave you, Ruth says. Where you go, I will go. Where you sleep, I will sleep. Your people will be my people. Your God will be my God. Where you die, I will die. Naomi sees that Ruth means it. She stops arguing. The two women walk on together.

This chapter begins with Ruth's promise. It is the story of a stranger who chose to stay. Then it turns to another woman, Hannah, who prayed for a child. Her son Samuel would grow up to lead Israel. And the chapter ends with the people asking for something new: a king.
story.think: Ruth could have gone home like Orpah. Why do you think she stayed with Naomi instead? What did it cost her?

lessons.title: A Famine and a Journey
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Ruth says a family left Bethlehem in a famine, and Naomi came back with only Ruth beside her.
reading: The book of *Ruth* is short. It has only four chapters. It begins in the days when the judges judged. There was a famine, a time with no food. A man from Bethlehem took his wife *Naomi* and two sons to the land of Moab. Moab was across the Dead Sea, to the east.

In Moab, Naomi's husband died. Her sons married Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. Then both sons died too. Naomi heard that there was food again in Bethlehem. She decided to go home. Her sons' wives started out with her.

On the road, Naomi told them to go back. Orpah went back. Ruth stayed. When they reached Bethlehem, the women of the town were surprised. Naomi told them not to call her Naomi, which means pleasant. She said to call her Mara, which means bitter. Her life had been very hard.

words.d: a Moabite woman who stayed with Naomi; also the short book that tells her story
Ruth's mother-in-law, who went to Moab in a famine and came home to Bethlehem
a land east of the Dead Sea; the book of Ruth says Naomi's family lived there

look.title: Pleasant or Bitter?
look.text: In Hebrew, the name Naomi is close to a word meaning pleasant. When Naomi comes home, she says: Do not call me Naomi. Call me Mara, which means bitter. Picture the women of Bethlehem hearing this. They knew her years ago, when she left with a husband and two sons. Now she is back with one young woman from Moab.
look.prompt: Why does Naomi want a new name? What has changed for her? What has she not lost?

check.q: Why did Naomi's family leave Bethlehem, according to the book of Ruth?
choices: They wanted to see the sea
check.why: Ruth 1:1 says there was a famine in the land, and the family went to Moab to find food.

check.q: Where was Moab?
check.why: Moab was a land east of the Dead Sea, across from Judah.

check.q: What name does Naomi ask to be called when she comes home?
check.why: Naomi says to call her Mara, which means bitter, because her life had been so hard.

lessons.title: Where You Go, I Will Go
lessons.mainIdea: Ruth's promise to Naomi is one of the best-known lines in the Tanakh, and Jewish tradition reads it as a choice to join the people of Israel.
reading: On the road, Ruth made a *promise*. She said she would go where Naomi went. She would live where Naomi lived. Naomi's people would be her people. Naomi's God would be her God. She would die where Naomi died. Only death would part them.

Ruth was a Moabite. She was not born into the people of Israel. Jewish tradition reads her words as a choice to join them. The rabbis of the Talmud and the midrash saw Ruth as a model of a person who becomes Jewish by choice. In Hebrew, such a person is called a *ger*.

Many readers notice what Ruth puts first. She does not say she will get a better life. She says she will stay with Naomi. Loyalty comes before anything else. The book of Ruth never uses the word love for the two women. It shows it instead.

words.d: words that bind you to do something; Ruth's promise was to stay with Naomi
in Jewish tradition, a person who joins the Jewish people by choice; Ruth is a model

look.title: Ruth's Promise
look.text: And Ruth said: 'Entreat me not to leave thee, and to return from following after thee; for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God;
look.prompt: "Entreat" means beg. "Whither" means where. Count how many things Ruth promises in this one verse.

check.q: What does Ruth promise Naomi in Ruth 1:16?
choices: To go where she goes and stay with her
check.why: Ruth 1:16 says where you go, I will go, and your people shall be my people.

check.q: In Jewish tradition, what is a ger?
choices: A person who joins the Jewish people by choice
check.why: A ger is a person who becomes Jewish by choice. The rabbis read Ruth as a model of one.

check.q: What comes first in Ruth's promise, as many readers notice?
check.why: Ruth does not ask for anything for herself. She says she will stay with Naomi no matter what.

lessons.title: Gleaning in the Fields
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Ruth says Ruth gathered leftover grain, a practice the Torah set up to feed the poor, in the field of a man named Boaz.
reading: Ruth and Naomi came to Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest. They had no food. Ruth said she would go *glean*. To glean is to pick up grain that the harvesters drop or leave behind. The Torah says farmers must leave some grain for the poor and the stranger.

Ruth went to a field. It belonged to a man named *Boaz*. He was a relative of Naomi's husband. Boaz noticed Ruth. He had heard how she stayed with Naomi. He told his workers to let her glean safely. He told them to drop extra grain on purpose.

Ruth worked all day. She came home with a big load of barley. Naomi asked whose field it was. When she heard the name Boaz, she was glad. Boaz was family. In the book, gleaning is not just about food. It shows how the Torah's laws about the poor worked in a real field.

words.d: to gather grain left behind by harvesters; the Torah says it is for the poor and the stranger
the field owner in the book of Ruth, a relative of Naomi's husband
a grain harvested in spring; Ruth gleaned barley in Boaz's field

look.title: Leave Some for the Poor
look.text: Leviticus 19:9–10 tells farmers not to harvest all the way to the corners of their fields, and not to go back for what was dropped. The corners and the fallen grain are to be left for the poor and for the stranger.
look.cite: Leviticus (Vayikra) 19:9–10, paraphrased from the Jewish Publication Society translation, 1917
look.prompt: Ruth was both poor and a stranger. How does this law from the Torah help explain what she does in Boaz's field?

check.q: What does it mean to glean?
choices: To sell grain at a market
To gather grain the harvesters left behind
check.why: Gleaning is picking up leftover grain. The Torah says it must be left for the poor and the stranger.

check.q: Who owned the field where Ruth gleaned?
check.why: Ruth 2 says the field belonged to Boaz, a relative of Naomi's husband.

check.q: What did Boaz tell his workers to do for Ruth?
check.why: Boaz told his workers to let Ruth glean safely and to leave extra grain for her.

lessons.title: Boaz the Redeemer
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Ruth says Boaz acted as a redeemer, married Ruth, and their great-grandson was King David.
reading: In the Torah, a close relative could help a family that lost its land or its men. Such a helper was called a *go'el*, a redeemer. Naomi knew Boaz was a relative. She sent Ruth to ask him to be their redeemer. Ruth went at night to the threshing floor, where grain was beaten out.

Boaz said he was willing. But there was a closer relative. Boaz went to the town gate, where business was done. He asked the other man in front of ten elders. The man said no. So Boaz took off his sandal, an old sign of a deal, and agreed to redeem the family.

Boaz married Ruth. They had a son named *Obed*. The women of the town said a son had been born to Naomi. The book ends with a family list. Obed was the father of Jesse. Jesse was the father of David. So Ruth, the stranger from Moab, was the great-grandmother of Israel's most famous king.

words.d: a redeemer; a close relative who helps a family that has lost its land or its men
the son of Ruth and Boaz; the book says he was the grandfather of David

look.title: From Ruth to David
look.text: Read the chain at the end of the book of Ruth like a set of steps. Ruth and Boaz have a son, Obed. Obed has a son, Jesse. Jesse has a son, David. David becomes the king remembered in the Psalms. Now go back to the dusty road. Ruth, a Moabite, was told to go home.
look.prompt: Why might the book end with this family list? What does it say about who can belong to the people of Israel?

check.q: What is a go'el?
choices: A redeemer, a relative who helps a family
check.why: A go'el is a redeemer. Boaz took on that role for Naomi and Ruth.

check.q: Where did Boaz settle the matter with the closer relative?
choices: At the town gate, in front of elders
check.why: Ruth 4 says Boaz went to the town gate, where business was done, and spoke before ten elders.

check.q: How is Ruth related to King David, according to the book?
check.why: The book ends: Obed, son of Ruth, was the father of Jesse, who was the father of David.

lessons.title: Ruth and Shavuot
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish tradition reads the book of Ruth on Shavuot, the spring harvest holiday that also remembers the giving of the Torah.
reading: In the Tanakh, the book of Ruth is not next to Judges. It is in *Ketuvim*, the Writings, the third part. It is one of five short books called the *Megillot*, or scrolls. Each of the five is read on a different holiday. Ruth is read on *Shavuot*.

Shavuot comes seven weeks after Passover. Its name means weeks. It was a harvest holiday for wheat and the first fruits. Jewish tradition also says the Torah was given at Mount Sinai on Shavuot. Many Jewish families eat dairy foods, like cheese blintzes, on this day.

Why read Ruth on Shavuot? Readers give a few reasons. The story happens during the harvest. Ruth chose to accept the Torah, just as the people did at Sinai. And Jewish tradition says King David, Ruth's great-grandson, was born and died on Shavuot. In Chicago and around the world, synagogues read this scroll each spring.

words.d: the Writings, the third part of the Tanakh; the book of Ruth is in it
five short books in Ketuvim, each read on a holiday; Ruth is one of them
the holiday seven weeks after Passover; the harvest and the giving of the Torah

look.title: Counting to Shavuot
look.cite: Leviticus 23:15–16, Jewish Publication Society translation, 1917; common Jewish practice
look.prompt: Seven weeks is forty-nine days. What number day is Shavuot? Why might a harvest holiday be a good day to read a story about a field?

check.q: In which part of the Tanakh is the book of Ruth?
check.why: Ruth is in Ketuvim, the third part, as one of the five Megillot, not next to Judges.

check.q: On which holiday is the book of Ruth read?
check.why: Jewish tradition reads Ruth on Shavuot, the harvest holiday seven weeks after Passover.

check.q: What does Jewish tradition say happened on Shavuot at Mount Sinai?
check.why: Jewish tradition teaches that the Torah was given at Sinai on Shavuot.

lessons.title: Hannah's Prayer
lessons.mainIdea: The first book of Samuel says Hannah prayed quietly for a child, and the rabbis made her prayer a model for how to pray.
reading: The book of *1 Samuel* begins with a woman named *Hannah*. She was married to Elkanah. She had no children. This made her very sad. Every year the family went to the holy place at Shiloh. One year, Hannah went to the door of the sanctuary and prayed.

Hannah made a promise. If God gave her a son, she would give him back to serve God all his life. She prayed with her lips moving, but no sound came out. The priest *Eli* saw her. He thought she was drunk. Hannah said no. She was pouring out her heart.

Eli blessed her. The text says Hannah had a son. She named him *Samuel*. When he was a small boy, she brought him to Shiloh to live with Eli, as she had promised. The rabbis of the Talmud pointed to Hannah. They said prayer should be like hers: quiet, from the heart, with the lips moving.

words.d: the woman in 1 Samuel who prayed for a son and promised him to God
the priest at Shiloh who blessed Hannah and raised Samuel
Hannah's son, who became a prophet and judge; also the name of two books in Nevi'im

look.title: How Hannah Prayed
look.text: In the Talmud, tractate Berakhot 31a, the rabbis learn rules for prayer from Hannah in 1 Samuel 1:13. She spoke in her heart, so a person praying should mean it inside. Her lips moved, so a person should form the words. Her voice was not heard, so prayer should be quiet.
look.cite: Talmud, Berakhot 31a, paraphrased from Rodkinson's translation, 1896–1903; 1 Samuel 1:13, JPS 1917
look.prompt: The rabbis turned a story into rules. Find each rule and the part of Hannah's story it comes from.

check.q: What did Hannah promise if she had a son?
choices: To bring him a new coat
To give him back to serve God
check.why: 1 Samuel 1:11 says Hannah promised to give her son to serve God all his life.

check.q: What did Eli think when he saw Hannah praying?
check.why: Eli saw her lips move with no sound and thought she was drunk; she told him she was pouring out her heart.

check.q: Why do the rabbis of the Talmud point to Hannah?
choices: Her prayer is a model: quiet and from the heart
check.why: Berakhot 31a learns rules for prayer from how Hannah prayed in 1 Samuel 1.

lessons.title: A Voice in the Night
lessons.mainIdea: The text says young Samuel heard a voice calling his name at night, and Eli taught him how to answer.
reading: Samuel grew up at Shiloh. He helped Eli, who was old and could not see well. One night Samuel was lying down near the *ark*, the holy box that held the tablets. He heard a voice call his name. He ran to Eli and said, here I am. Eli said he had not called.

This happened three times. The third time, Eli understood. He told Samuel to lie down again. If the voice came, Samuel should say: speak, for your servant is listening. The voice came a fourth time. Samuel answered as Eli had said.

The text says the message was hard. Eli's sons had done wrong, and Eli had not stopped them. Samuel was afraid to tell Eli. In the morning, Eli made him tell everything. Eli accepted it. From then on, the book says, all Israel knew Samuel was a *prophet*, a person who speaks for God.

words.d: here, the holy box at Shiloh that held the tablets; not Noah's boat
a person the text says speaks for God; Samuel became one

look.title: Speak, I Am Listening
look.text: And the LORD came, and stood, and called as at other times: 'Samuel, Samuel.' Then Samuel said: 'Speak; for Thy servant heareth.'
look.prompt: "Heareth" means hears. Who taught Samuel to answer this way? Why might it matter that he says he is listening, not talking?

check.q: Where was Samuel when he heard the voice, according to 1 Samuel 3?
check.why: 1 Samuel 3 says Samuel was lying down in the sanctuary at Shiloh, where the ark was.

check.q: Who told Samuel how to answer the voice?
check.why: The third time, Eli understood and told Samuel to say: speak, for your servant is listening.

check.q: What is a prophet in the Tanakh?
choices: A person who speaks for God
check.why: A prophet is someone the text says speaks for God. After that night, all Israel knew Samuel as a prophet.

lessons.title: Samuel the Judge
lessons.mainIdea: The text says Samuel was the last of the judges, traveling from town to town to lead the people.
reading: Samuel grew up to be a judge, like Deborah and Gideon. But he was also a prophet. The book says he traveled in a circle each year. He went to Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah. In each place he judged the people. Then he went home to Ramah.

The Philistines were still a danger. The text says they once captured the ark in battle. Eli died when he heard the news. Later, Samuel gathered the people at *Mizpah*. He prayed for them. The text says the Philistines were driven back.

Samuel set up a stone to remember that day. He called it Eben-ezer, which means stone of help. Readers often call Samuel the last judge. After him, the book turns to kings. Jewish tradition counts 1 and 2 Samuel as two parts of one book, named for him.

words.d: the town where the text says Samuel gathered the people and prayed
stone of help; the name Samuel gave a stone to remember a victory

look.title: Samuel's Yearly Circle
look.prompt: Why might a judge travel to different towns instead of staying in one place? Think about who could reach him.

check.q: What did Samuel do in Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah each year?
check.why: 1 Samuel 7:16 says Samuel went in a circle to these towns and judged Israel in each place.

check.q: What does Eben-ezer mean?
check.why: Samuel named the stone Eben-ezer, stone of help, to remember the victory at Mizpah.

check.q: Why do readers call Samuel the last judge?
choices: After him, the book turns to kings
check.why: Samuel led as a judge, and then, 1 Samuel says, the people asked for a king.

sections.title: The People Ask for a King

lessons.title: Give Us a King
lessons.mainIdea: The book of 1 Samuel says the people asked Samuel for a king like other nations, and Samuel warned them what a king would take.
reading: Samuel grew old. His sons were judges, but the text says they were not honest. The elders of Israel came to Samuel at Ramah. They said: give us a king to judge us, like all the *nations*. Samuel did not like this. He prayed about it.

The text says God told Samuel to listen to the people. But Samuel should warn them first. So Samuel told them what a king would do. A king would take their sons for his army. He would take their daughters as workers. He would take the best of their fields and a tenth of their crops.

The people still said they wanted a king. They wanted someone to lead them in battle. Samuel agreed. Later, the text says, he poured oil on the head of a tall young man named *Saul*. This was called anointing. Saul became the first king. The next chapter tells his story.

words.d: other peoples with their own lands and rulers; Israel asked for a king like theirs
the tall young man the text says Samuel anointed as Israel's first king
to pour oil on someone's head as a sign they are chosen to lead

look.title: What a King Will Take
look.text: In 1 Samuel 8:11–17, Samuel warns the people. A king will take their sons to drive his chariots and run before him. He will take their daughters to cook and bake. He will take the best fields and vineyards and give them to his servants. He will take a tenth of their grain and flocks. And the people, Samuel says, will be his servants.
look.cite: 1 Samuel 8:11–17, paraphrased from the Jewish Publication Society translation, 1917
look.prompt: The people heard this warning and still wanted a king. Why do you think they did? Was Samuel right to warn them?

check.q: What did the elders ask Samuel for?
check.why: 1 Samuel 8:5 says the elders asked for a king to judge them, like all the nations.

check.q: What did Samuel warn a king would do?
choices: Take their sons, daughters, fields and crops
check.why: In 1 Samuel 8, Samuel lists what a king takes: sons, daughters, fields and a tenth of the crops.

check.q: What does it mean to anoint someone?
choices: To pour oil on their head as a sign they are chosen
check.why: Anointing means pouring oil on the head. The text says Samuel anointed Saul as the first king.

lessons.title: Chesed, the Thread
lessons.mainIdea: The Hebrew word chesed, loyal kindness, runs through the stories of Ruth, Hannah and Samuel.
reading: There is a Hebrew word that runs through this chapter. The word is *chesed*. It is hard to say in one English word. It means kindness, but more than that. It means kindness that keeps a promise. It means loyalty. The JPS 1917 translation often says kindness or mercy.

The book of Ruth uses the word three times. Naomi hopes God will show chesed to Ruth and Orpah. Naomi says Boaz has shown chesed to the living and the dead. Boaz tells Ruth her chesed is great. Ruth stayed when she did not have to. That is chesed.

Hannah kept her promise and gave up her son. Eli accepted hard news with grace. Samuel served the people all his life. Jewish tradition calls chesed one of the things the world stands on, in Pirkei Avot 1:2. Readers say the book of Ruth is a story of chesed from start to end.

words.d: loyal kindness; kindness that keeps a promise even when it costs something
staying true to a person or a promise, the way Ruth stayed with Naomi

look.title: What the World Stands On
look.text: In Pirkei Avot 1:2, Simeon the Just is quoted as saying the world stands on three things: on the Torah, on worship, and on acts of loving-kindness, in Hebrew gemilut chasadim.
look.cite: Pirkei Avot 1:2, paraphrased from Charles Taylor, Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, 1877
look.prompt: Pick one person from this chapter. Which of the three things in this saying did they do? Give one example from the text.

check.q: What does chesed mean?
choices: Loyal kindness that keeps a promise
check.why: Chesed is kindness joined with loyalty, like Ruth staying with Naomi when she did not have to.

check.q: Who does Boaz say has shown great chesed?
check.why: In Ruth 3, Boaz tells Ruth that her kindness, her chesed, is great.

check.q: In Pirkei Avot 1:2, what are the three things the world stands on?
choices: Torah, worship and acts of loving-kindness
check.why: Simeon the Just's saying names Torah, worship and acts of loving-kindness, gemilut chasadim.

review.q: Why did Naomi's family go to Moab?
review.why: Ruth 1:1 says a famine sent the family from Bethlehem to Moab.

review.q: Which of these is part of Ruth's promise in Ruth 1:16?
choices: I will build you a house
Your people shall be my people
I will go back to Moab
review.why: Ruth says: where you go, I will go; your people shall be my people; your God, my God.

review.q: Who was the great-grandson of Ruth and Boaz?
review.why: The book of Ruth ends: Obed was the father of Jesse, and Jesse was the father of David.

review.q: On which holiday do Jewish communities read the book of Ruth?
review.why: Ruth, one of the five Megillot, is read on Shavuot, the harvest holiday.

review.q: How did Hannah pray at Shiloh?
review.why: 1 Samuel 1:13 says Hannah spoke in her heart; her lips moved but her voice was not heard.

review.q: What did Eli tell Samuel to say to the voice?
choices: Speak, for your servant is listening
Where you go, I will go
review.why: 1 Samuel 3:9 says Eli told Samuel to answer: speak, for Thy servant heareth.

review.q: Whom did Samuel anoint as the first king of Israel?
review.why: 1 Samuel 10 says Samuel anointed Saul, a tall young man, as Israel's first king.

review.q: Which word best describes Ruth staying with Naomi?
review.why: Boaz calls Ruth's loyalty chesed, kindness that keeps a promise at a cost.
